approach: Average acceleration is the velocity change over the interval, and velocity at any time is the starting velocity plus the area under the a-t graph up to that time.

steps.text: Find the change in velocity from t = 6 s to 12 s as the signed area under the a-t graph, a trapezoid from a = 20 to a = −10.
Divide by the 6 s interval for the average acceleration.
Build up the velocity from t = 0 by adding the area under each segment of the a-t graph in turn.
Add the area of the final segment, t = 12 s to 14 s, to get the velocity at t = 14 s.

common_mistakes.text: Treating the acceleration as constant at its t = 6 s value of 20 m/s² for the whole 6 s to 12 s window, instead of the actual straight-line decrease, gives v(14) = 180 m/s.
